transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-07
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jenna Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Banerjee (Northstar Eng Manager), Diego Ramos (Northstar CTO), Elliot Chan (Northstar SRE)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Northstar is evaluating Redwood for a customer-facing inference surface with strict SLOs for 99th percentile latency and multi-region availability requirements.
- Primary concerns: fallback behavior on region/zone failures, SLA definitions for hosted vs dedicated, KV cache priming across replicas, and data residency/policies.
- Agreed next steps: exchange traffic profile, Redwood to propose SLO acceptance criteria and a runbook, run a performance benchmark.

Topics: SLO targets, fallback policies, multi-region routing, Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs, audit/logging, cost implications.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Alex from Redwood, Samir and Jenna on the SE side.
[00:08] Priya (Northstar): Hi, Priya here, Diego and Elliot also with me. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:12] Alex: Awesome. Today we want to understand your acceptance criteria for reliability and what you expect from fallbacks and multi-region routing. Priya, do you want to kick off with the high-level problem?
[00:22] Priya: Sure. Our app serves realtime product recommendations to users in EU and NA. We have a 99.9% availability target per region and 99p latency under 250ms for the happy path. But from a SRE perspective we also need deterministic behavior when a region loses capacity — we need clear fallback rules, not just best-effort.
[00:38] Diego: Also, regulatory note: EU customer data should not leave region except for telemetry that is aggregated and anonymized. So any cross-region failover needs to be auditable.
[00:47] Samir (Redwood SE): Got it. When you say fallback rules, are you thinking automatic cross-region failover or degrading to a lighter model in-region? Or both?
[00:54] Elliot (SRE): Both. For brief capacity spikes we'd prefer in-region degradation — like going to a smaller model or cached response — rather than routing to another region which complicates compliance. But for full-region outages we need cross-region failover with explicit approval windows.
[01:10] Jenna (Redwood SE): That aligns with Redwood's routing policies. We support policy-based routing: prefer local, if local capacity is below a threshold then try compatible model variants in-region (quantized), then if still constrained and policy allows, fallback to an approved remote region. Policies are fully auditable.
[01:26] Priya: Quick question — how does that interact with KV cache and session affinity? We have some stateful prompts where warm KV cache matters a lot for latency.
[01:35] Samir: Good call. KV cache priming is sticky to a container/replica. For cross-region fallbacks we either accept a cold start (higher latency) or we implement prefix caching — Redwood can sync hot prefixes to remote pop nodes ahead of failover for an approved set of keys. There's a tradeoff of cost and staleness.
[01:55] Diego: Right, we can't afford frequent cross-region sync because of cost and consistency. We need the runbook to outline thresholds and expected cold-start penalties.
[02:03] Alex: We'll include cold-start numbers from prior benchmarks in the playbook. Jenna, can you summarize the multi-stage fallback that Samir described?
[02:10] Jenna: Sure — Stage 0: Local instance healthy; Stage 1: Local degraded — switch to quantized / smaller model variant in-region; Stage 2: Serve from local prefix cache (if hit); Stage 3: If still failing and policy allows, route to approved remote region with audit log; Stage 4: Graceful degradation responses (e.g., shorter completion, cached template) if remote route unavailable.
[02:34] Priya: How do you detect 'degraded'? Is it latency-based, queue-depth, or instance health checks?
[02:40] Samir: You can configure multiple signals. Typical setup is combination: sustained 95p latency > threshold plus instance CPU/GPU utilization and pending request queue depth. We provide a scoring function and recommend thresholds based on your traffic distribution.
[02:52] Elliot: Can the scoring function be adjusted per endpoint? We have different classes — search autocomplete needs 99p 120ms, long-form generation can tolerate more.
[03:00] Jenna: Yes, per-route SLOs are common. You can pin routes to models and routing policies. Redwood Console shows per-route SLO breaches and can trigger runbook steps automatically or via an operator approval gate.
[03:14] Diego: SLA question — hosted vs dedicated. If we go hosted with Redwood, what's your SLA on latency and uptimes? We need contractual language.
[03:23] Alex: For hosted we typically quote best-effort with published performance profiles; enterprise SLA for uptime is part of the dedicated and private contracts. Dedicated comes with a 99.95% uptime SLA and latency SLOs depending on model class. We can add credits for sustained breaches.
[03:38] Diego: And private deployments? On-prem or VPC — same SLA?
[03:42] Samir: Private is typically customer-managed infra, so Redwood provides the control plane SLA and operational playbooks; the infra SLA depends on the customer's environment. For air-gapped or on-prem we offer an enterprise package with runbook support and onboarding assistance.
[03:57] Priya: About auditing — we need full trails for model selection and routing decisions for compliance. Is that included?
[04:03] Jenna: Yes, per-request routing decisions, model variant chosen, fallback triggers, and any operator approvals are recorded in the audit log. You can export logs or integrate with your SIEM via streaming.
[04:12] Priya: Good. For cost modeling, if we do local quantized fallback vs remote full model, how do we estimate cost impact?
[04:19] Alex: Redwood Optimize gives estimated token-cost and compute-cost per route. We can run scenario modeling — e.g., X% of traffic hits Stage 1 quantized variant, Y% cold-start to remote — to project monthly spend. We'll include a simple spreadsheet in the next email.
[04:33] Elliot: We definitely want that. Also, can we implement a manual override to stop cross-region failover during business hours?
[04:41] Samir: Yes, there are operator gates. Policies can be automated or require manual approval. You can also set blackout windows per region.
[04:49] Priya: On the technical deep dive side, we also want to understand failover latency typical numbers. Do you have historical metrics for a cold remote fallback to NA from EU?
[04:58] Jenna: From past perf runs, cold remote fallback averages 800-1200ms p99 for medium-length prompts due to KV cache miss and routing hops; warm fallbacks with prefix priming can be under 200-300ms. We'll supply benchmark artifacts.
[05:12] Priya: That's a big delta. We'll need to capture expected user-visible behavior in the runbook.
[05:17] Diego: Security note — any failover to remote region must have encryption at rest and in transit, and KMS keys must be auditable. Our legal team will ask about where keys reside.
[05:26] Alex: Redwood supports KMS integration and customer-managed keys for Dedicated and Private. In hosted we have BYOK options with HSM integration for enterprise tiers. We'll surface a short security doc.
[05:36] Elliot: Also, are there options for partial failover where only non-PII prompts route remote? We want to minimize cross-border PII exposure.
[05:44] Samir: You can tag routes and enforce policies at route-level. Filtering or tokenization at the edge before routing is a recommended pattern. We can integrate with your pre-processing layer to scrub or mask PII before routing.
[05:57] Priya: Great. One more thing — our traffic is very bursty; we require graceful throttling behavior and clear backpressure semantics. How does Redwood handle that?
[06:06] Jenna: We expose token-level throttles and queueing. In Dedicated you can configure reserved concurrency and burst capacity. A typical pattern is a leaky-bucket queue and tail-drop with explicit error payloads telling the app to fallback to cached templates.
[06:22] Alex: For SLA acceptance, what would be your success criteria for the pilot? Priya, Diego?
[06:29] Priya: Pilot success: (1) Meet per-route 99p latency targets for at least 30 days under a representative load; (2) Demonstrate deterministic fallback behavior with documented runbook; (3) No compliance violations during failover test.
[06:43] Diego: Add: runbook response times for operator acknowledgements under 15 minutes for critical incidents.
[06:49] Alex: Noted. We'll draft acceptance criteria accordingly.
[06:55] Elliot: How invasive is instrumentation? We already have Prometheus and Datadog.
[07:00] Samir: Redwood can emit metrics to Prometheus remote-write and push events to Datadog. We can also surface traces and per-request IDs for correlation.
[07:08] Priya: Okay. Any examples of customers who did similar multi-stage fallbacks?
[07:13] Jenna: We ran a pilot with a retail customer (name redacted) who used in-region quantized fallback for traffic spikes and kept cross-region failover for outages; it reduced cost by 22% while keeping 99p availability.
[07:26] Diego: Sounds promising. On procurement timeline — if the pilot succeeds we aim to sign Dedicated contract by end of Q2.
[07:34] Alex: That feels realistic. We'll align proposal timelines to your procurement windows.
[07:39] Priya: Let's talk about a concrete test scenario for the benchmark. We want a controlled induced failure in EU zone A to test Stage 1-3 behaviors. Can Redwood run a chaos test sim?
[07:49] Samir: Yes, we can run a chaos sim in a staging environment to emulate zone loss and capture routing decisions, cold-starts, and audit logs. We recommend running it with your traffic replay to be most realistic.
[08:02] Priya: We'll prepare a traffic replay. Can you also expose the runbook steps as a machine-readable playbook (yaml) we can integrate with our ops runbook?
[08:11] Jenna: Absolutely. Our rollout and runbook definitions are exportable YAML with decision trees and operator commands.
[08:18] Diego: On the legal side, we want retention periods for audit logs—how long do you retain routing logs in hosted?
[08:25] Alex: Hosted default is 90 days; enterprise packages can extend to 2 years with archival. We'll include options and costs.
[08:33] Priya: Any blockers from Redwood's side to running the benchmark next week?
[08:38] Jenna: We just need your traffic profile and a list of routes with SLOs. Also, a preferred window for the chaos sim.
[08:45] Priya: We'll send that by Thursday.
[08:48] Alex: Great. Quick recap and next steps — I’ll read them out and then open to any final Qs.
[08:54] Alex: Redwood action items: send SLO acceptance draft and fallback playbook, cost scenario spreadsheet, provide benchmark artifacts and schedule perf run. Northstar action items: share traffic histogram, list of routes and SLOs, confirm chaos sim window.
[09:09] Diego: One last question: if we start hosted and then move to Dedicated, how smooth is the migration for pinned models and keys?
[09:18] Samir: We support model pinning and versioning; migration path includes a compatibility check and replayed traffic tests. Keys need re-provisioning for Dedicated/Private but we support BYOK so it's standard. Migration typically takes a few weeks depending on data residency constraints.
[09:33] Priya: Thanks. That helps. No further questions from our side.
[09:36] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the SLO draft by Wednesday EOD and get the benchmark scheduled.
[09:44] Priya: Thanks all. Bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional name and product nouns may be misrecognized (e.g., 'prefix cache' transcribed as 'press fix cache' in raw automations). Manual corrections applied to clarify key technical terms.
